title: Inspections and the licensee
body: Licensees aren't inspectors. Recommend that buyers get professional inspections, give a list of several qualified inspectors, and let the buyer choose. Never discourage an inspection.
example: A Las Vegas buyer's agent gives three inspector names and lets the buyer pick.

title: As is isn't a hiding place
body: Selling as is means the seller won't repair. It doesn't excuse hiding known defects. Anything found in a pre-listing inspection becomes known to the seller and must be disclosed.
example: A Reno seller sells as is but still discloses the known cracked heat exchanger.
hook: As is limits repairs, not honesty.

title: Lead-based paint (pre-1978)
body: For housing built before 1978, sellers and landlords must disclose known lead hazards, give the EPA pamphlet, and use the required disclosure. Buyers get 10 days to test unless they waive it. Agents must make sure it's done.
example: A 1965 home in Reno's Old Southwest gets the federal lead disclosure before the buyer signs.

title: Other hazards to know
body: Radon is a soil gas found only by testing. Asbestos is dangerous when friable and may be encapsulated. Mold signals moisture. Leaking underground tanks contaminate soil. Carbon monoxide comes from faulty fuel-burning appliances.
example: A Carson City buyer tests for radon during escrow and adds a mitigation fan.
hook: Test for what you can't see.

title: Disclose material facts
body: Sellers and licensees must disclose known material facts, especially latent defects. Red flags, like stains or cracks, should be disclosed and investigated, not ignored.
example: A Henderson listing agent sees fresh paint over a ceiling stain and asks the seller about past leaks.
hook: See a red flag? Say so.

title: Stigmatized properties
body: A death, crime, or reputed haunting doesn't change the building, but can affect buyers. State law decides what must or needn't be disclosed. Federal law treats HIV/AIDS as a disability, so it must not be disclosed.
example: Nevada has its own rules on stigmatized property. You'll learn them in the Nevada units.

title: PETE: government's four powers
body: Police power regulates use for health and safety. Eminent domain takes property for public use with just compensation. Taxation funds government. Escheat passes property to the state when there's no heir.
example: Nevada widens a highway near Fernley and pays owners for the strips of land it takes.
hook: PETE: Police, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat.

title: Property taxes and special assessments
body: Property taxes are ad valorem, meaning based on value. Special assessments charge only the properties that benefit from a specific improvement, like new curbs. Both become liens with priority.
example: Henderson adds sidewalks on one street and assesses only those owners.
hook: Special assessment: you benefit, you pay.

title: Master plans and zoning
body: A master plan sets the long-range vision. Zoning ordinances carry it out by setting uses, density, height, and setbacks. Building codes set construction standards, enforced by permits and inspections.
example: Clark County's zoning allows a duplex on one Las Vegas lot but not on the one next door.
hook: Plan the vision, zone the rules, code the building.

title: Exceptions to zoning
body: A variance lets an owner deviate because of hardship. A conditional use permit allows a special use with conditions. A nonconforming use was legal before a zoning change and may continue. Spot zoning for one owner's benefit is usually invalid.
example: A corner store in a Reno neighborhood rezoned residential may continue as a nonconforming use.
hook: Variance bends the rule. Nonconforming came first.

title: Superfund liability
body: Under CERCLA, current and past owners can be responsible for cleanup costs even if they didn't cause the contamination. A Phase I environmental assessment before buying supports the innocent landowner defense.
example: An investor buying an old North Las Vegas gas station orders a Phase I first.
hook: Buy the dirt, buy the dirt's problems.

title: Wetlands and flood zones
body: Filling wetlands generally needs a federal permit. FEMA maps flood zones. In a Special Flood Hazard Area, federally backed loans require flood insurance.
example: A Las Vegas home near a wash sits in a mapped flood zone, so the lender requires flood insurance.
hook: Flood zone plus federal loan equals flood insurance.

title: Private restrictions
body: CC&Rs and deed restrictions are private limits on use, recorded and binding on later owners. When a private rule and zoning conflict, the stricter one applies. Discriminatory restrictions are unenforceable.
example: Zoning allows two stories, but the Summerlin CC&Rs limit homes to one. The CC&Rs control.

title: Covenants vs. conditions
body: Breaking a covenant usually leads to an injunction or damages. Breaking a condition can cost the owner the property. Courts prefer covenants because forfeiture is harsh.
example: A Henderson owner builds an unapproved wall. The HOA gets an injunction to remove it.
hook: Covenant: court order. Condition: you could lose it.
